headline: Double Creek fluke bite holds steady as bunker blitzes light up Barnegat Inlet
subhead: Weakfish have gone deep and quiet for August, but fluke on the channel edges and bluefish at the inlet are keeping rods bent.
body_markdown:
I had a kid on the boat this week, maybe nine years old, asking me why we were running the edge of Double Creek Channel instead of anchoring up on the flat where his dad said the fluke were thick back in June. I told him what I've been telling people for forty years — the bay doesn't sit still just because the calendar says summer. Come the first week of August, with the flats baking under afternoon sun and water temps up where nothing wants to be shallow past ten in the morning, the fish slide off into the channels and hold there until the tide or the hour drags the bait back up. That kid caught his first keeper fluke twenty minutes later in eleven feet of water on the drop-off past the "S" turn, and I got to feel like I knew something again.

That's about the size of it out there right now. The bay is carrying its full August heat load — warm on top, a little cooler down where the current scours the channel bottom — and that thermal split is doing most of the work for us. Double Creek Channel has been the most consistent thing I've fished all week, drifting the deeper bend in twelve to sixteen feet on the last two hours of the incoming and the first hour of the outgoing, when the current's still got some shape to it but isn't ripping. Four-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on three-quarter ounce bucktails, tipped with a sliver of squid, dragged slow along bottom — that's been the winning combination. Keepers to five pounds, a lot of just-short fish mixed in, which tells me there's a decent class of fluke coming up behind this year's crop. Slack water kills it dead, so time your drift around the moving water, not the clock.

Weakfish I have to be honest about — they've gone quiet the way they always do once the water gets properly warm. The May run at the sedge banks feels like a different season entirely. What few weakfish anyone's finding now are holding deep, off the mouth of Oyster Creek and down along the channel edges toward Waretown, and they're coming on bait — bloodworms or a live killie under a slip sinker — fished right on bottom in the cooler pockets. It's not a bite worth planning a whole trip around this week. If you connect, treat it as a bonus, not the plan.

Bluefish are where the real energy's been. Bunker schools have piled up thick in the bay this month, and every tide change at Barnegat Inlet has been producing surface blitzes — birds working, blues busting bait right up against the rocks on the north side. I flagged this pattern last week, said the building tidal push toward the new moon would sharpen up the current-driven spots, and that's exactly what's happened at the inlet. Metal — Deadly Dicks, Kastmasters in the one-to-two ounce range — thrown right into the froth on the outgoing has been about as easy as bluefishing gets. Bring wire leader or you'll donate more lures than you keep. These blitzes have been short-lived, ten, fifteen minutes at a crack, so when you see the birds start dropping, don't dawdle getting over there.

Blowfish and kingfish are doing their quiet August thing, which for those two species means steady rather than spectacular. Blowfish are stacked up in the deeper holes off Barnegat Light and around the channel markers near Tices Shoal, biting on small pieces of clam or squid fished on a simple two-hook rig right on the bottom. It's not glamorous fishing but it fills a cooler for a shore dinner, and it's about the most reliable thing going for kids and grandkids who want steady action without a lot of technique. Kingfish have been working the sandy stretches just inside the inlet and along the edges of Island Beach, small strips of bloodworm or squid on a high-low rig in eight to fifteen feet of water. Nothing big, but a plate of kingfish fillets never disappointed anybody.

We had a run of those typical early-August thunderstorm afternoons this week too — the kind that shut the surface bite down cold for two or three hours and then hand it right back on the evening tide. That's held true again this year, same as it does most Augusts, and it's worth building your day around. Mornings and evenings have simply outfished the middle of the day, storms or no storms.

Looking ahead, the new moon on the 12th is going to push more water through this bay than we've seen in a couple of weeks, and that stronger tidal flow should sharpen up everything current-related — the inlet blitzes, the channel-edge fluke bite, even the blowfish holes where a little extra push moves bait past them. If I had one day to fish this coming week, I'd want the two hours around the inlet tide change with metal ready for blues, then slide back into Double Creek on the tail of that same tide for fluke before the sun gets too high. It won't be a banner week for weakfish no matter what you do, but the rest of the program is holding up fine for the middle of August.
